Metadata.title: AnyThingISee — Local disassembler and decompiler for Windows
Metadata.description: A free analysis tool to read x64 PE and ELF files as linked C pseudocode and assembly, keep names and notes, and export patches.

hero.title: Disassemble, decompile and patch with <u>AnyThingISee</u>
hero.body: AnyThingISee is a local binary analysis tool that runs right on Windows. Read C pseudocode and assembly side by side, line by line, for x64 PE and ELF files, and handle names, notes and instruction patches in one view. The Ghidra native decompiler core is built in, so there's no Ghidra or Java to install, and your files never leave your PC.
hero.warning: Seeing a warning on install? · Check SHA-256

items.title: Light install
items.body: The Ghidra native decompiler core is built in, so there's no Ghidra or Java to install. All you need on Windows is .NET Framework 4.6.2 and WebView2.

items.title: Stays on your PC
items.lead: Your files are never sent anywhere
items.body: All analysis happens on your own machine, so you can open binaries you can't share with anyone else.

items.title: Originals untouched
items.lead: Opening doesn't run it, patching doesn't overwrite it
items.body: Opening a file for analysis never runs the target program. Patches are saved to a separate file, leaving the original as is.

items.title: Results with evidence
items.lead: Know what to trust and what to check
items.body: Every function shows the evidence it was found by, and instructions not recovered into C are marked, so you review the uncertain parts first.

items.title: Free, even for work
items.body: Use the Free Edition at no cost, including for work and commercial purposes. The current version will never be made paid retroactively.

items.title: In your language
items.body: The interface comes in three languages. The command palette (Ctrl+K) and shortcuts let you run anything without digging through menus.

steps.title: Open a file
steps.body: Choose a file or drop it onto the window.

steps.title: Pick a function
steps.body: Select a function on the left and read C and assembly together.

steps.title: Keep names and notes
steps.body: Create a project to keep renames and notes. Press F2 to rename.

steps.title: Export a patch
steps.body: Edit instructions and export the result to a separate file.

items.a: Yes. Individuals and organizations can use the current Free Edition at no cost, including for commercial work. A future paid edition will not retroactively charge for this free version.
The AnyThingISee source is not published. Bundled third-party components, such as the Ghidra native decompiler, keep their own licenses.

items.q: Windows shows a warning when I install.
items.a: The installer is not code-signed yet. Check the SHA-256 and the download source on the download page. You don't need to turn off any security features.

items.q: Can I trust the decompiler output?
items.a: This is a preview and complete recovery is not guaranteed for every binary. Verify types, conditions, call arguments and return values against the original assembly before relying on them.
Only Windows 10/11 x64 is supported today. A macOS (Apple Silicon) version is in development.

items.q: Have you compared it with other tools?
items.a: We are measuring it against Ghidra, IDA Free, Binary Ninja Free and Cutter under the same conditions. Results will be published on the comparison page together with the environment, versions, date and sample binaries.
Open a GitHub issue with the product version, Windows version, steps to reproduce and the error. Don't attach private binaries or personal data.

items.label: C pseudocode
items.title: Read assembly and C line by line
items.body: Pick a function to open its assembly and C pseudocode side by side. The instruction addresses behind the selected C line show up right away.
points: The C recovery map shows which instructions are linked to C and which aren't
Unrecovered spans are marked, so you review what not to trust first
The inspector shows function discovery evidence and incoming and outgoing references

items.label: Flow graph
items.title: Follow branches as a graph
items.body: Each function is split into basic blocks and drawn as a control-flow graph. Select a block and the inspector shows references for that address.
points: Taken, not-taken, unconditional and fall-through edges differ by line style and color
Every block shows its start address and kind (branch, jump)
Jump between assembly, C pseudocode and bytes at the same address

third.title: Third-party components
third.lead: The Free Edition license does not restrict the rights these components' licenses grant.
third.ghidraNote: Ghidra is developed by the National Security Agency and its contributors. Its native core is embedded in AnyThingISee and is not represented as original AnyThingISee code. The complete Ghidra application and Java runtime are not included.
third.webviewNote: The Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime is a prerequisite supplied separately by Microsoft. The installer includes WebView2 SDK components only.

Compare.title: Benchmarks
Compare.metaDescription: How AnyThingISee compares with Ghidra, IDA Free, Binary Ninja Free and Cutter under the same conditions, and how we measured.
Compare.lead: We only publish values we measured ourselves on the same PC with the same samples. Every number comes with the environment, versions and date.

pending.title: Measurements in progress
pending.body: There are no results to publish yet. Results will appear here once measurements following the method below are complete.

Compare.ghidraNote: AnyThingISee embeds the Ghidra 11.4.3 native decompiler core, so its decompiler output and speed may be close to Ghidra's.

method.title: Method
items: Measured on a single Windows 11 x64 machine; CPU, RAM, disk and build number are recorded.
Public, redistributable PE and ELF binaries in several sizes, with SHA-256 and source published.
Each metric is run at least 3 times and the median is used.
Tools that are GUI-only are timed manually, and marked as such.
